title: CTO Interview with Ed Plowman of Imagination Technologies
gist: Imagination Technologies CTO Ed Plowman argues the binding constraint is converting TOPS into useful delivered work within power/thermal/cost envelopes, and that rapid AI model churn favors programmable, adaptable GPU-style compute plus heavy software investment over over-specialized NPUs, especially in long-lifecycle automotive.

insights.claim: Imagination Technologies CTO Ed Plowman argues customers' biggest challenge is not generating more TOPS but turning TOPS into useful work, since memory bandwidth, data movement, utilisation, latency and software overhead matter as much as theoretical compute.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Datasheet TOPS is a weak proxy for edge AI competitiveness; evaluate system-level utilisation and software.
insights.quote: The biggest challenge is not generating more TOPS. It is turning those TOPS into useful work.

insights.claim: Edge and automotive SoCs must run graphics, computer vision, AI inference, sensor processing and conventional software concurrently within fixed power, thermal and cost envelopes, so all workloads compete for the same resources.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Mixed-workload efficiency favors architectures that share resources flexibly.
insights.locator: Customers are trying to run graphics

insights.claim: Imagination Technologies deliberately biases toward adaptable, programmable compute rather than hardening silicon around today's workload, because AI model architectures and data formats change in months while chip development cycles take years.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Supports a GPU-first IP strategy versus fixed NPU IP vendors.
insights.quote: Model architectures, data formats and optimisation techniques can change in months, while semiconductor development cycles are measured in years.
insights.locator: Why is your approach to solving

insights.claim: Dedicated neural processing hardware is extremely efficient only while workload assumptions hold; the more specialized the silicon, the more certain one must be about the workload, and AI currently offers little such certainty.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Fixed-function NPU designs carry obsolescence risk if model architectures shift.
insights.quote: the more specialised you become, the more certain you need to be about the workload
insights.locator: What other approaches are being used

insights.claim: Ed Plowman acknowledges tightly integrated, vertically controlled hardware-software stacks have produced very impressive results, particularly in cloud AI.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Implicit nod to vertically integrated incumbents' dominance in cloud, with Imagination positioning for edge instead.

insights.claim: The key architectural decision is where to draw the line between specialization, programmability and efficiency, and how expensive it is to move that line later.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A useful lens for evaluating any accelerator vendor's roadmap risk.
insights.locator: So it is really a question

insights.claim: Automotive amplifies AI architectural risk because validation and safety cycles take years and vehicles stay in market over a decade, so architectural bets today target workloads that may not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Automotive OEMs may favor programmable compute IP to hedge against model churn over long vehicle lifecycles.
insights.quote: You are effectively making architectural bets today against workloads that may not properly exist yet.

insights.claim: Over-specializing silicon too early risks turning today's optimization into tomorrow's constraint as AI workloads change.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Watch for stranded NPU silicon as a risk factor in edge/auto chip suppliers.
insights.quote: Over-specialise too early and today’s optimisation can become tomorrow’s constraint.
insights.locator: That is why I keep coming back

insights.claim: Imagination Technologies no longer treats AI as a separate market but as part of nearly every market it serves and increasingly part of graphics itself.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: GPU IP vendors can frame AI as an expansion of their core graphics TAM rather than a new segment.
insights.locator: How has AI changed your business strategy

insights.claim: Ed Plowman says the bigger opportunity is often in software—compilers, tooling, workload mapping and using AI to optimize applications for the architecture—because software gaps cannot be bridged by adding engineers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Software stack maturity is the differentiator to diligence for edge AI IP vendors.
insights.quote: You cannot bridge every software gap simply by throwing more engineers at it.
insights.locator: It has also changed how I think
